Feedback: - H9 Over-applied formatting rule [measured 9/14 runs passed over 3 tasks]: Specify a non-default formatting rule for a base metric (e.g., thousands separators for visitor counts), but leave the formatting of a derived metric (e.g., average daily visitors) unstated. Display both on the same output line. The agent will over-apply the base metric's formatting to the derived metric, failing the strict spec where the default formatting (no separators) was expected. Evidence: museum-exhibition-schedule-checklist 0/5: all five runs failed by applying thousands separators to the average daily visitors, over-applying the rule stated only for 'visitor counts'.

Feedback: - Strict inequality filtering (strictly greater than) and inverted priority semantics (1=highest) are intermittently missed: agent defaults to >= comparisons and higher-number-higher-priority, and its self-tests often use boundary values that don't distinguish > from >= or don't test priority ordering with data revealing inverted semantics (evidence: 7 tasks with 0-2/5 failures on these rules)

Feedback: - A15 Contradictory example output [untested]: Ensure the worked example output exactly matches the format specification; if the spec lists fields A, B, C, D but the example only shows A, B, D for some instances, agents will be confused about whether to follow the spec or the example, and all runs will fail regardless of implementation quality. Evidence: warehouse-robot-task-log-summary 0/5: the example output omitted 'Total Items' for RB02 while the format specification listed it as a required field, causing all 5 runs to fail even when agents identified the inconsistency and followed the written rules

Feedback: - H11 Counter-default requirement [measured 47/67 runs passed over 15 tasks]: State a requirement that contradicts the obvious default implementation (e.g., case-insensitive grouping when case-sensitive is the default; showing a single date when a range is the default; first-seen spelling when last-occurrence-wins deduplication would suggest using the surviving entry's spelling). Ensure the test inputs include cases where the default behavior would produce different output, so agents that implement the default will fail. Crucially, ensure the provided worked example does NOT exercise this counter-default requirement, so the agent cannot catch the bug by testing its code against the example. Evidence: manifest-migration-report-checklist 1/5: all failing runs produced wrong output for inputs where case-sensitive grouping, always-show-range, or post-deduplication spelling defaults would differ from the stated requirements

Feedback: - A19 Unspecified error message format [untested]: When the spec requires error messages to stderr but doesn't specify the exact format (e.g., 'Line X: [error]' vs 'Invalid record at line X: [error]'), either document the expected format explicitly or accept any reasonable format that conveys the error type and location. Evidence: patch-compliance-reporter (run 3): the spec says 'Messages about invalid records are written to stderr' without specifying format, but the test expected 'Line X: [error]' while the agent output 'Invalid record at line X: [error]', causing a false failure on an unspecified requirement.

Feedback: - A18 Unstated log replay interactions [untested]: When designing event log replay tasks, explicitly state the expected behavior for overlapping events (e.g., whether a second RENTAL before a RETURN replaces the first or is ignored, and whether the first is discarded or closed with a default duration), and explicitly state whether to output entities with zero counts; omitting these causes agents to assume all events are valid and all entities are output. Evidence: bike-share-log-replay-checklist 0/5: all failing runs counted a replaced rental as 60 minutes (2 rentals instead of 1) and output bikes with zero rentals, because the instruction did not specify what happens to a RENTAL when another RENTAL occurs for the same bike, or whether to output bikes with ze

Feedback: - A14 Ambiguous format template without worked example [untested]: When the output format template uses placeholders (qty, $price, disc%) without specifying exact formatting (decimal places, spacing, $-prefix conventions, percentage format) and provides no worked example showing the exact expected output string, agents cannot verify their formatting and will consistently fail even when all processing rules are correctly implemented. Always include at least one complete worked example with the exact expected output, including edge cases like zero discounts and amounts crossing the comma-separator threshold. Evidence: auto-detail-receipt-checklist 0/5: all 5 runs failed because the format template was ambiguous about exact value formatting and no worked example was provided, causing agents to guess differently on discount decimal places, $-prefix conventions, and item-line spacing.

Feedback: - H10 Mixed-direction sort [measured 6/20 runs passed over 4 tasks]: Require sorting by one field ascending and another field descending; agents often apply reverse=True to the whole comparison tuple or key, reversing both fields instead of just the required one. Evidence: museum-exhibition-schedule-checklist (runs 1, 3): failing runs sorted both start date and name in reverse by applying reverse=True to the whole tuple, misunderstanding the mixed-direction sort requirement.

Feedback: - A16 Ambiguous bracket notation in format spec [untested]: When specifying output format templates, do not use [variable] notation for placeholders; agents may interpret brackets as literal characters. Use a worked example showing the exact literal output, or use {variable} / <variable> notation, or describe the format in prose without brackets. Evidence: swim-lesson-schedule-checklist-export (run 5): failing run wrapped date and time in literal square brackets ([10/02/2024] [09:00]) because the format spec used [date] [time] notation that was ambiguous between placeholder and literal brackets.

base_prompt:
You author ORIGINAL Harbor tasks for evaluating a coding agent (GLM-5.3-flash with high reasoning, a terminal agent with Python 3.12). The agent sees instruction.md and the files in /app; hidden pytest tests in /tests check the final state afterwards.

GOAL: an EASY task (a careful engineer finishes it in 5-15 minutes) containing TWO or THREE independent, plainly stated details that a reader on autopilot gets wrong, each from a different trap family below. Target: the agent solves it in 1-3 of 5 attempts.

MEASURED ON THE FIRST TASKS OF THIS FAMILY: a single trap that the instruction emphasises (bold text, a 'Note', a stated reason such as 'because that is where overnight stock is held', or the detail repeated in the return-value description) is caught every time: the agent passed 5/5. Each detail must therefore be stated exactly ONCE, mid-paragraph, in an ordinary sentence: no bold, no 'note', 'important', or 'must', no explanation of why, no repetition elsewhere. Because each detail is caught most of the time on its own, combine two or three independent details so that missing any one of them fails.

WHY (measured on ~150 runs of this agent): it implements explicit requirements carefully and verifies everything it can check, so large, complex, or deep tasks only make it run out of time, which measures nothing. Its repeatable wrong answers come from autopilot: it recognises a familiar task, writes the textbook solution, checks it against its own understanding, and signs off confidently, skimming past the one stated detail that changes the answer. Public evidence agrees: modified versions of classic puzzles (models answer the familiar version), and goal-implied constraints such as "I want to wash my car and the car wash is 50 m away: walk or drive?" (most models say walk).

TRAP FAMILIES (use the one named in FOCUS; invent a NEW instance, never reuse a published puzzle, riddle, or benchmark item):
1. Modified classic: the task looks like a very familiar algorithm or chore (interval merging, LRU cache, change-making, word frequency, run-length encoding, binary search, rate limiting, grid flood fill, leap years, Roman numerals, round-robin scheduling, deduplication, pagination), but the instruction states ONE change that alters the answer on most inputs (for example: intervals that only touch do NOT merge; evict the most recently used entry; ties go to the later record; words are case-sensitive). The textbook solution must fail most hidden tests.
2. Constraint implied by the goal: the purpose of the task implies a constraint that the obvious computation ignores, like the car needing to be at the car wash. Examples of the shape: a van must end its route at the depot that holds tomorrow's stock; a retention policy must never delete the only copy of a month; a meeting must fit the organizer's own availability. State the purpose plainly; once noticed, the constraint is unambiguous.
3. Stated non-default convention: dates written day-first, decimal commas, half-open ranges, 1-based numbering, weeks starting on Monday, a stated non-UTC zone, a non-alphabetical sort order. State it once in a normal sentence; the default makes the answer wrong.
4. Fencepost and counting language: "every 3rd day starting today", "a post every 2 m along a 10 m fence including both ends", "between 5 and 9 exclusive". The natural off-by-one reading is wrong.
5. Stated rule that differs from the language default: the requirement is ordinary business logic, but Python's default does something else, so the reflexive one-liner is wrong: halves round up (Python's round() rounds half to even), negative quantities truncate toward zero (// floors), remainders take the sign of the dividend (% takes the divisor's), consecutive delimiters produce empty fields (str.split() collapses whitespace), "file9" sorts before "file10" (sorted() is lexicographic), amounts are compared in exact cents (floats drift). Inputs where the default and the rule agree must not dominate the hidden tests.
7. Silent data-visible edge case: the instruction states only a general fact ("a payment is identified by its payment_id", "the ids were copy-pasted from emails and may contain invisible characters", "the export has the same format as /app/data/sample.csv", "rows are individual line items"), and a sample data file in /app/data (a reference file at data/<name>) contains the rare cases that make the natural implementation SILENTLY wrong: re-sent duplicates of the same id, zero-width or look-alike characters in identifiers, a unit or scale stated only in the header (for example "amount (k€)"), TOTAL or subtotal rows mixed into the data, continuation lines, or a column whose meaning changes after a marker row. The natural implementation must run without errors on the sample and produce plausible numbers; only actually inspecting the data reveals the issue, and once seen, the correct handling follows from the stated fact. Hidden tests generate files containing the same patterns. MEASURED: when the edge case was not determinable from anything the agent could see, 2 of 5 runs failed, but that is unfair; this family makes the edge case visible in the data instead.
8. Checklist breadth: ONE easy-looking task (a formatter, exporter, or summariser over small inputs) with 8-12 independent small requirements, each stated once in plain words and each one of the measured slip types: rounding mode, inclusive/exclusive bound, day-first dates, natural or stated sort order with a tie-break, case/whitespace normalisation, thousands separators, empty-field handling, singular/plural wording, trailing newline, a stated non-default default value. Every hidden input exercises several requirements, and every requirement is exercised by several inputs. MEASURED: each single stated detail is missed in about 3-7% of runs (only in rushed runs), so about ten independent details are needed to land near a 50% pass rate; keep every requirement trivial so the task stays short.
6. Perspective and self-inclusion counting: a count seen from one member's point of view must include or exclude that member or a related one (like "Alice has 3 brothers and 2 sisters; how many sisters does her brother have?" where Alice herself counts). Use realistic data: teams, households, org charts, group chats.

FAIRNESS (strict):
- A careful human reading the instruction gets the right answer without guessing. The trap detail is written plainly in instruction.md (or docs it references); never hidden in comments, never misleading, never contradicted elsewhere.
- No ambiguity: exactly one correct behaviour for every hidden test input.
- No resource the container lacks (no network, no dictionaries beyond the standard library).
- No checker, reference implementation, or example in /app or in the instruction that exercises the trap: worked examples must use inputs where the trap does not matter, so the agent cannot discover its mistake by testing.

DESIGN:
- instruction.md: short and natural, like a real ticket (8-25 lines). Each trap detail appears once, in an ordinary sentence among other ordinary requirements, not emphasised and not explained. Describe the return value neutrally: never restate a trap detail there. Frame the task so it strongly evokes the familiar textbook task.
- The worked example (if any) must give the same output under the textbook reading and the correct reading, so it neither reveals nor confirms any trap.
- The agent implements a function or CLI in /app (for example /app/solution.py with a documented function signature). Hidden tests call it on 15-30 inputs, most of which exercise the trap, so the answer cannot be guessed and the textbook approach fails most of them; a few inputs where the trap does not matter make a partially correct solution look plausible.
- reference_files: the correct solution file. The starter replaces the core function body with a stub: ONE BUG block whose FIND is the entire correct function body and whose REPLACE is a docstring plus `raise NotImplementedError`.
- tests/test_outputs.py: pytest; embed an independent reference implementation and generate the hidden inputs deterministically (fixed seeds or literal lists); compare exactly; import the agent's module from /app.
- META must include "trap": one sentence per trap naming the detail and the autopilot mistake, and "hint": one plain sentence that restates ALL trap details prominently (the pipeline appends it to the instruction only if the task proves too hard). Hidden tests: most inputs exercise at least one trap, and every trap is exercised by several inputs.

The task must be original and different from the already-generated tasks listed by the user.

OUTPUT FORMAT. Reply ONLY with these blocks, in this order. Write file contents verbatim; each block header is a line of its own.

=== META ===
{"slug": "short-kebab-case-descriptive-name", "summary": "one sentence", "trap": "one sentence", "hint": "one sentence", "strategies": ["H1"]}
=== FILE instruction.md ===
<verbatim markdown>
=== FILE README.md ===
<short plain-language overview for humans; do not reveal the trap>
=== FILE app/<path relative to /app> ===
<correct reference file; repeat for every application file>
=== FILE tests/test_outputs.py ===
<verbatim pytest module>
=== BUG b1 <path relative to /app> ===
<<<FIND
<the entire correct function body, occurring exactly once>
>>>REPLACE
<docstring plus raise NotImplementedError>
>>>TRAP
<the stated detail the agent must not miss>
>>>CLASS
<trap family name>
=== END ===

# Solver profile p019

Built from 326 recorded probes at 2026-10-07 19:09.

## Strengths
- Reliably implements entire methods from specification including complex algorithms like dynamic programming for route optimization (evidence: 20+ tasks)
- Employs extensive ad-hoc verification with inline Python test scripts covering edge cases, randomized differential testing, and example validation (evidence: 25+ tasks)
- Consistently compiles code before submission using py_compile (evidence: 20+ tasks)
- Achieves 4-5/5 on compound tasks with 9-11 independent formatting/computation rules when boundary conditions are explicitly testable, including DD/MM/YYYY dates, half-up rounding, reverse-alphabetical tie-breaks, thousands separators, natural sort, title case, and accounting formatting (evidence: 15+ tasks)
- Can correctly implement strict inequalities and inverted priority semantics when these non-default rules are caught and explicitly tested during self-verification (evidence: 11 tasks including tasks with priority-1-is-highest, urgency-descending, and strict-greater-than filters)

## Weaknesses
- Overconfident self-assessment: routinely claims "all tests passed" or "verified" and submits despite missing bugs, even after writing extensive tests (evidence: 11 tasks with 0/5 scores where agent claimed verification)
- Verification tests share blind spots with implementation: self-written tests encode the same rule misunderstandings as the code, producing false confidence (evidence: 11 tasks where agent's tests passed but grading failed)
- Consecutive delimiters indicating empty fields cause systematic failure because agent defaults to split() which collapses whitespace, losing empty fields between delimiters (evidence: 1 task with 0/5 across all runs)
- Compound tasks with 10+ independent non-default rules show consistent 0/5 failure rate because agent cannot track and verify all deviations from programming defaults simultaneously (evidence: 4 tasks)
- Strict inequality filtering (strictly greater than) and inverted priority semantics (1=highest) are intermittently missed: agent defaults to >= comparisons and higher-number-higher-priority, and its self-tests often use boundary values that don't distinguish > from >= or don't test priority ordering with data revealing inverted semantics (evidence: 7 tasks with 0-2/5 failures on these rules)
- Column names containing unit hints (e.g., 'annual_fee_cents') cause the agent to skip required unit conversion, treating cent values as dollar values (evidence: 2 tasks from previous profile)

## Hypotheses
- When implementing from scratch (not fixing a provided buggy implementation), the agent is more likely to miss non-default rules because it encodes its default assumptions into both implementation and tests → Design a task with 8-9 non-default rules where the agent must write the entire function body, compared to a variant where a buggy implementation is provided for fixing
- Self-tests rarely include boundary-distinguishing values (e.g., testing exactly-at-threshold vs. one-above-threshold to distinguish > from >=) → Design a task where the only difference between correct and incorrect is whether value 5 passes a "greater than 5" filter, and the example input includes exactly 5
- Processing order dependencies (filter before dedup vs. dedup before filter) are missed when the spec states the order but the agent's tests use data where both orders produce the same result → Design a task where filtering must precede deduplication, with test data containing duplicates that would survive dedup but fail the filter
- Multi-step computations where intermediate results must be stored and reused across processing stages are incorrectly implemented → Design a task where a discount threshold depends on the count of items passing a filter, and the discount applies to those same items after aggregation
- When a single task combines strict-inequality boundaries, inverted priorities, AND 8+ other formatting rules, the agent consistently misses the non-default semantic rules while correctly implementing the mechanical formatting rules → Design a task with strict > filter, priority-1-is-highest, and 8 standard formatting rules (DD/MM/YYYY, half-up rounding, thousands separators, etc.)

## Guidance
Place difficulty in combining strict inequality boundaries (> not >=), inverted priority/urgency semantics (1=highest not lowest), AND 8+ other independent rules to overwhelm the agent's capacity for tracking non-default behaviors. The agent's critical weakness is that its self-tests encode the same misunderstandings as its implementation, so include boundary values in the example that would distinguish > from >= (e.g., exactly 5 for a "more than 5" rule). Consecutive delimiters with empty fields is a reliable trap. Do not rely on accounting formatting, clear unit conversion without contradictory column names, half-up rounding alone, DD/MM/YYYY dates alone, or fewer than 8 independent rules as primary difficulty drivers, as the agent handles these reliably when they are the only non-default rules. The agent's self-assessment is never reliable proof of correctness.


STRATEGY LIBRARY (learned from every probe so far; pass rates are over tasks that used the strategy). Aim for an overall pass rate near 50%: the pass rate of a combination is roughly the product of its levers' measured rates (count an untested lever as 0.8), so pair one strong lever with one or two mild ones; when the focus line names REQUIRED LEVERS, build the task around exactly those. Strengthen weak levers as their notes suggest and never use an AVOID pattern. List the HARD strategy ids you used in META as "strategies": ["H1", ...].

HARD (lower the pass rate):
- H1 Counter-idiomatic stated exception [measured 17/24 runs passed over 5 tasks]: State a rule or exception that contradicts the obvious implementation (for example: tiles passed over during a forced movement do not trigger, only the tile where movement stops does; a blocked forced move still consumes the resource) and make it change the answer on several instances.
